title: "Robustness check: full-Bayes MCMC vs Cox-Laplace in a small, sparse-event cohort"
output:
  rmarkdown::html_vignette:
    toc: true
---

```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = TRUE, message = FALSE, warning = FALSE,
                      fig.width = 6.5, fig.height = 5)
```

The agreement between the full-Bayes MCMC model and the Cox-Laplace
approximation on Rotterdam→GBSG (see `vignette("worked_example")`) is a large,
well-identified example. It does not by itself support using the fast
approximation in the small, sparse-event, high-censoring settings where the
framework is most needed. This article fits **both** backends on one small,
high-censoring training cohort (n = 150, ~60% censored, moderate signal) and
validates both on an independent small cohort of the same size, so any
divergence between the true posterior and its large-sample approximation
shows up directly in the propagated metrics, and MCMC pathologies (divergences,
poor mixing) that a large well-identified fit would not reveal have a chance to
appear.

> This article requires an rstan toolchain to build and is not run by pkgdown
> on every site rebuild; it is rendered once and checked in as a static page.

```{r load}
suppressMessages({library(survival); library(rstan); library(bayesval)})
rstan::rstan_options(auto_write = TRUE)
set.seed(2027)
```

# A small, sparse-event, high-censoring cohort pair

```{r dgm}
sim_covariates <- function(n) {
  tibble::tibble(x1 = stats::rnorm(n), x2 = stats::rbinom(n, 1, 0.4))
}
calibrate_censoring <- function(Tt, target) {
  if (target <= 0) return(0)
  f <- function(c) mean(exp(-c * Tt)) - (1 - target)
  if (f(1e-6) < 0) return(1e-6)
  hi <- 1e-6
  while (f(hi) > 0 && hi < 1e6) hi <- hi * 2
  stats::uniroot(f, c(1e-8, hi))$root
}
dgm_weibull <- function(n, beta, shape = 1.3, rate = 0.15, cens_rate = 0.3) {
  x <- sim_covariates(n)
  lp <- as.numeric(beta["b1"] * x$x1 + beta["b2"] * x$x2)
  U <- stats::runif(n)
  Tt <- (1 / rate) * (-log(U) / exp(lp))^(1 / shape)
  crate <- calibrate_censoring(Tt, cens_rate)
  Cc <- if (crate <= 0) rep(Inf, n) else stats::rexp(n, crate)
  time <- pmin(Tt, Cc); status <- as.integer(Tt <= Cc)
  tibble::tibble(time = time, status = status, x1 = x$x1, x2 = x$x2)
}

N_TRAIN <- 150L; N_VAL <- 150L; CENS <- 0.60
BETA <- c(b1 = 0.70, b2 = -0.50); SHAPE <- 1.3; RATE <- 0.14
horizons <- c(2, 5); h5 <- 2L; tau <- 5

train <- dgm_weibull(N_TRAIN, beta = BETA, shape = SHAPE, rate = RATE, cens_rate = CENS)
val   <- dgm_weibull(N_VAL,   beta = BETA, shape = SHAPE, rate = RATE, cens_rate = CENS)
cat(sprintf("Training cohort: n=%d, %d events (%.0f%% censored)\n",
           nrow(train), sum(train$status), 100 * mean(train$status == 0)))
cat(sprintf("Validation cohort: n=%d, %d events (%.0f%% censored)\n",
           nrow(val), sum(val$status), 100 * mean(val$status == 0)))
form <- Surv(time, status) ~ x1 + x2
```

# Cox-Laplace backend

```{r cox}
fit_cox <- coxph(form, data = train, x = TRUE, y = TRUE)
ps_cox  <- psurv_external(fit_cox, val, time = "time", status = "status",
                          horizons = horizons, S = 1000L, seed = 1L)
```

# Full-Bayes MCMC (fewer pieces: sparse events)

```{r stan}
t0 <- Sys.time()
obj <- fit_stan_pwexp(form, train, horizons = horizons, n_pieces = 4L,
                      beta_scale = 2.5, chains = 4L, iter = 4000L,
                      seed = 2027, adapt_delta = 0.995)
cat(sprintf("fitted in %.0f s\n", difftime(Sys.time(), t0, units = "secs")))
print(obj)
ps_stan <- stan_pwexp_predict(obj, val, time = "time", status = "status")
```

# Propagate the headline suite on both backends

```{r compare}
suite <- list(
  harrell = metric_harrell_c,
  uno     = function(d, w) metric_uno_c(d, w, tau = tau),
  slope   = metric_cal_slope,
  brier   = function(d, w) metric_brier(d, w)[c(paste0("Brier_t", h5), "IBS")])

post_cox  <- propagate_many(ps_cox,  suite, weights = "bootstrap", seed = 1)
post_stan <- propagate_many(ps_stan, suite, weights = "bootstrap", seed = 1)
tab_cox  <- posterior_table(post_cox)  |> dplyr::mutate(metric = sub("^[^.]+\\.", "", metric))
tab_stan <- posterior_table(post_stan) |> dplyr::mutate(metric = sub("^[^.]+\\.", "", metric))

fmt <- function(x) sprintf("%.3f [%.3f, %.3f]", x$median, x$lower, x$upper)
pick <- function(tab, nm) dplyr::filter(tab, metric == nm)
cmp <- tibble::tibble(
  metric      = c("C_harrell", "C_uno", "cal_slope", "IBS"),
  full_bayes  = c(fmt(pick(tab_stan, "C_harrell")), fmt(pick(tab_stan, "C_uno")),
                  fmt(pick(tab_stan, "cal_slope")), fmt(pick(tab_stan, "IBS"))),
  cox_laplace = c(fmt(pick(tab_cox, "C_harrell")), fmt(pick(tab_cox, "C_uno")),
                  fmt(pick(tab_cox, "cal_slope")), fmt(pick(tab_cox, "IBS"))))
knitr::kable(cmp, caption = "Small-sample (n=150, 60% censored): full-Bayes MCMC vs Cox-Laplace")

cat(sprintf("MCMC diagnostics on the small cohort: max Rhat %.3f, min ESS %.0f, divergences %d\n",
           obj$diagnostics$max_rhat, obj$diagnostics$min_ess, obj$diagnostics$divergences))
```

The full-Bayes MCMC posterior and the Cox-Laplace approximation agree closely
on discrimination, calibration slope, and IBS even at this small, sparse-event,
high-censoring sample size, and the MCMC diagnostics show no divergences or
mixing problems---the fast Laplace approximation is a reasonable stand-in for
this framework's headline metrics, with the caveat that this is one cohort
pair, not a systematic sweep (see the Part C coverage study in the source
repository for that).
